name: Magnesium (serum)
summary: The magnesium dissolved in blood serum, under 1% of the body's total; the body holds it in a fairly tight range by drawing on bone and adjusting kidney losses, so serum levels fall late in a deficit.
why_it_matters: Magnesium is a cofactor for hundreds of enzymes, including those that make and use ATP, and it helps regulate heart rhythm, muscle and nerve function, blood pressure and insulin signalling. In cohort studies, lower serum magnesium is associated with higher rates of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, atrial fibrillation and cardiovascular disease. The conventional lab lower limit (about 0.75 mmol/L) was set from the distribution in a 1970s US population sample, not from health outcomes, and expert groups have proposed raising it to 0.85 mmol/L.

ref_range.source: Conventional lab range, derived from NHANES I (1971-1974) population data; ranges vary by lab
ref_range.note: Many labs use lower limits of 0.65-0.70 mmol/L (1.6-1.7 mg/dL). mg/dL = mmol/L / 0.4114; mEq/L = mmol/L x 2.

optimal.source: Rosanoff et al., Eur J Nutr 2022 (MaGNet consensus); Costello et al., Adv Nutr 2016
optimal.rationale: Expert groups in the US and Germany independently proposed 0.85 mmol/L (2.07 mg/dL) as the lower cut-off, because serum levels below it are associated with higher risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease in outcome studies. The 0.85-0.95 mmol/L range is a proposal, not yet adopted by most labs. In NHANES 2021-2023, roughly two-thirds of US adults sit below 0.85 mmol/L.

deep:
## What it is

An adult body holds roughly 20-28 g of magnesium, about half in bone, most of the rest inside muscle and other cells. Serum carries under 1% of it. The kidneys and bone buffer serum levels tightly, so serum magnesium can stay in the conventional range while total-body stores are low; this is sometimes called chronic latent magnesium deficiency.

## Why the lower limit is debated

The widely used reference range of 0.75-0.95 mmol/L comes from the serum distribution in NHANES I (1971-1974), a sample of apparently healthy US adults. A range built that way describes what is common, not what is healthy, and it would include people already low in magnesium.

- **Costello et al., 2016** reviewed outcome data and argued for an evidence-based reference interval, noting that subclinical deficiency can exist within the current range.
- **Rosanoff et al., 2022** (an international MaGNet consensus) recommended **0.85 mmol/L (2.07 mg/dL)** as the lower cut-off for defining low magnesium, with an evidence-based range of 0.85-0.95 mmol/L. US and German groups had reached the same figure independently. Of 43 lab reference ranges they surveyed, only 2 used 0.85 mmol/L or higher as the lower limit.
- A 2025 position paper in *Magnesium Research* (Weisser, Kisters, Vormann, von Ehrlich, Micke) repeats the call to standardize the lower limit at 0.85 mmol/L, or at least note on lab reports that levels below it are associated with higher disease risk.

These associations come from observational studies; they do not by themselves show that raising serum magnesium lowers risk.

## What moves it

- **Diet:** leafy greens, legumes, nuts, seeds and whole grains are the main sources; refined diets are low.
- **Medications:** long-term proton pump inhibitors, loop and thiazide diuretics, some antibiotics and chemotherapy agents increase losses.
- **Alcohol, poorly controlled diabetes, diarrhea or malabsorption** increase losses.
- **Kidney disease** can raise serum magnesium, especially with magnesium-containing laxatives or antacids.
- **Sample handling:** hemolysis falsely raises the result, because red cells contain more magnesium than serum.

## What to test alongside

Potassium and calcium (low magnesium makes both harder to correct), creatinine/eGFR, and in some settings a 24-hour urine magnesium. Red-cell magnesium is offered by some labs but is less standardized.

## References

- Costello RB, Elin RJ, Rosanoff A, et al. Perspective: The Case for an Evidence-Based Reference Interval for Serum Magnesium: The Time Has Come. *Adv Nutr*. 2016;7(6):977-993. [PubMed 28140318](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28140318/)
- Rosanoff A, West C, Elin RJ, et al. Recommendation on an updated standardization of serum magnesium reference ranges. *Eur J Nutr*. 2022;61(7):3697. [PMC9186275](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9186275/)
- Weisser H, Kisters K, Vormann J, von Ehrlich B, Micke O. Serum magnesium concentration: time for a standardised and evidence-based reference range. *Magnes Res*. 2025;38(2):41-44.
